title: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK): The Limbal Battleground
summary: A crescent-shaped, destructive inflammation of the peripheral corneal stroma characterized by epithelial defect, stromal thinning, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Often a precursor to lethal systemic vasculitis, PUK requires urgent multidisciplinary intervention to prevent both ocular perforation and systemic morbidity.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is a serious inflammatory condition of the peripheral cornea. It is characterized by a crescentic 'juxtalimbal' ulceration with an overlying epithelial defect and stromal melting (lysis). Unlike simple marginal keratitis, PUK involves the destruction of the corneal collagen matrix and is frequently driven by an underlying systemic autoimmune process.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Limbal Microenvironment
content: Step 1: Systemic circulating immune complexes (Type III Hypersensitivity) or Autoantibodies (Type II) reach the limbal vasculature.
Step 2: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1) upregulate adhesion molecules on limbal vessel endothelium.
Step 3: Massive recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the peripheral corneal stroma.
Step 4: Release of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-9) and collagenases from the limbal conjunctiva and inflammatory cells.
Step 5: Rapid degradation of corneal Type 1 Collagen, leading to stromal melting and crescentic thinning.

rows: Vasculitis of the episcleral and limbal vessels.
Necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Intense ocular pain (often deep and boring, radiating to forehead).
Severe photophobia and lacrimation.
Decreased visual acuity (if visual axis involved or high astigmatism).
Crescent-shaped peripheral stromal thinning.
Active epithelial defect at the leading edge of the ulcer.
Associated scleritis or episcleritis (in 30-40% of cases).
Significant conjunctival and limbal injection.

branches: Type I: Benign, Unilateral, Elderly, Responds to local therapy
Type II: Malignant, Bilateral, Young (esp. African/Asian), Progressive
Diagnosis of Exclusion: NO systemic autoimmune disease

sections.title: Ocular Examination Checklist
content: Slit-Lamp: Assess depth of thinning (Descemetocele check).
Fluorescein: Map size of epithelial defect and undermining edges.
Scleral Exam: Check for 'bluish' hue (thinning) or necrotizing scleritis.
Gonioscopy: Evaluate for iris incarceration if perforation is suspected.
Imaging: AS-OCT to quantify residual stromal thickness precisely.

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Full Physical Exam: Check skin, joints, nose/throat, and lungs.
2. Blood Panel: CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, Anti-CCP.
3. Autoimmune Serology: ANA, ANCA (c-ANCA and p-ANCA).
4. Renal/Heme: Urinalysis (hematuria/proteinuria), Creatinine.
5. Imaging: Chest X-ray or CT Chest (look for GPA cavities).

rows: SLE or other connective tissue diseases

sections.title: Systemic Management Protocol
content: Induction: Oral Prednisone (1mg/kg/day) or IV Methylprednisolone pulse if impending perforation.
Steroid-Sparing Agents: Methotrexate (15-25mg/week), Azathioprine, or Mycophenolate Mofetil.
Biologic Therapy: Rituximab (anti-CD20) is now 1st line for GPA-associated PUK.
TNF Inhibitors: Infliximab or Adalimumab for refractory RA cases.
Monitoring: Co-management with Rheumatology for bone protection and marrow suppression.

sections.title: Ocular Management & Surgery
content: Preservative-free lubricants and topical antibiotics (prophylaxis).
Topical Medroxyprogesterone or Acetylcysteine (Collagenase inhibitors).
Avoid topical steroids (can accelerate melting/perforation).
Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For microperforations < 2mm.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting (AMT): Multilayer for tectonic support.
Crescentic Lamellar Keratoplasty: For severe thinning/structural loss.

sections.title: Red Flags & Critical Signs
content: Descemetocele: Imminent perforation (looks like a clear bubble in the ulcer).
Positive Seidel Test: Indicates full-thickness corneal perforation.
Necrotizing Scleritis: Severe associated scleral thinning and 'melting'.
Sudden loss of pain: Can paradoxically indicate total corneal anesthesia or perforation.
Unexplained Weight Loss/Hemoptysis: Suggests systemic vasculitis mortality risk.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Perforation & Endophthalmitis.
Secondary Glaucoma (inflammatory or steroid-induced).
Severe irregular astigmatism and corneal scarring.
Systemic Mortality: Untreated PUK in GPA has a 5-year mortality rate > 50%.
Cataract formation (due to chronic inflammation/steroids).

content.explanation: L: Limbal involvement, I: Inflammatory (Severe), M: Melting (Stromal), I: Immune-mediated (Systemic), T: Tectonic compromise.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Topical steroids are usually 'The Enemy' in PUK—they inhibit collagen synthesis and promote melting.
The limbal conjunctiva is the source of collagenases; surgical recession of the conjunctiva can sometimes slow the melt.
PUK may be the very first sign of a fatal systemic disease—treat the 'Eye as a Window' to the patient's survival.
Always check the nose and ears! GPA and Relapsing Polychondritis have distinct extraocular signs.
